analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates for large companies whose CEO earns over 50 times the median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, vote, or floor action since its September 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds a penalty of up to five percentage points to the standard 21% corporate tax rate, based on how many times more the CEO (or highest-paid employee) earns than the company's median worker. Companies paying their typical worker at least one-fiftieth of CEO pay keep the normal rate; the higher the gap above 50-to-1, the steeper the tax, reaching 26% at 500-to-1. It applies to public companies and private companies with $100 million or more in annual revenue, and it requires regulators to write rules stopping companies from dodging the ratio by replacing employees with contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that keep pay ratios at or below 50-to-1 gain a competitive advantage, and the federal Treasury gains revenue from the penalty. Workers at high-gap companies benefit indirectly: the tax gives their employers a financial reason to raise wages or trim executive pay rather than pay the surcharge. Ordinary taxpayers benefit to the extent the revenue is used to reduce taxes or deficits.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a graduated surcharge to the 21% corporate rate, rising from 0.5 points above a 50-to-1 pay ratio to 5 points above 500-to-1, so companies with the largest CEO-to-worker gaps pay the most.
Uses the pay-ratio figure public companies already report to the Securities and Exchange Commission, averaged over five years, so companies cannot game it with a single favorable year.
Extends the rule to private corporations with at least $100 million in average annual gross receipts, closing a loophole for large private firms, while exempting smaller companies.
Directs the Treasury Secretary to write anti-avoidance rules, specifically including manipulation of the ratio by using contractors instead of employees.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with the widest CEO-to-worker pay gaps pay higher federal taxes, up to 26% instead of 21%. Those costs could be passed to shareholders through lower profits, to executives through smaller compensation packages, or partially to consumers through prices. Large private companies also face new compliance costs to calculate and report their pay ratio.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big companies with wide pay gaps

drawbacks.text: The bill is a tax on the pay gap, not a wage mandate: companies may absorb the surcharge, shift pay to executives' equity outside the measured categories, or pass the cost to consumers rather than raise any worker's pay.

Averaging the ratio over five years means companies that widen pay gaps today face the penalty only gradually, and companies already cutting gaps this year get no credit until the rolling average catches up.
Large private companies with no SEC filing duty must build new pay-ratio calculations and reporting systems, a real compliance cost even for firms that ultimately avoid the tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is straightforward and hard to game in the main: it leans on a ratio companies already disclose, averages over five years, and includes an explicit anti-contractor rule. Its weakness is that it prices the pay gap rather than eliminating it; a company can decide a 1-5 point tax is cheaper than narrowing the gap. The revenue stream is real but modest relative to total corporate taxes, and the bill does not say how the revenue is used.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced the bill in September 2025 and the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, where it has had no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 16, 2025, by Sen. Sanders along with Democratic cosponsors Warren, Van Hollen, Markey, and Welch.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and the action history shows no further steps since.
The bill has five Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support in the record.
With Republicans holding the Senate majority and the Finance Committee chairmanship, the committee has taken no action in the months since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies with wide CEO-to-worker pay gaps are better off so far, because the surcharge has never advanced and would not take effect before 2026 even if it did.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is an independent who caucuses with Democrats, all five cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; Senate Finance is chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Large corporations with wide CEO-to-worker pay gaps
industries.note: These companies would pay a graduated surcharge of 0.5 to 5 percentage points on top of the 21% corporate rate; large public companies routinely report pay ratios far above 50-to-1. Their interest in avoiding the surcharge runs directly against the bill's goal of narrowing pay gaps.

They must calculate and report a pay ratio under Treasury rules for the first time, a compliance cost, and pay the surcharge only if their ratio exceeds 50-to-1. Companies below $100 million in receipts are exempt.

industries.industry: Human resources contractors and staffing firms
industries.note: The bill anticipates that companies may shift employees to contractor arrangements to shrink their measured pay ratio and directs Treasury to write anti-avoidance regulations; if enforcement falls short, staffing firms could gain business from pay-ratio arbitrage.

analysis.trajectory: A bill referred to Senate Finance with five progressive Democratic cosponsors, no Republican support, and no hearing has rarely reached a vote under this Congress's Republican majority; the realistic outlook is that it dies in committee when the session ends, unless pay-inequality politics shifts.
